nameStory: This little duck gets its name from the brilliant green patch, or speculum, that flashes across its wings when it flies. The word 'teal' itself comes from this very bird - it's the original source of the blue-green color name we use today! It's called 'green-winged' to distinguish it from other teal species that sport different colored wing patches.
description: The Green-winged Teal is one of our smallest dabbling ducks, about the size of a crow but stockier and built for water life. Males in breeding plumage sport a rich chestnut head with a distinctive green stripe swooping back from each eye, while females wear more modest mottled brown feathers. Both sexes flash that signature bright green wing patch when they take flight. These social little ducks love to gather in large flocks outside of breeding season, creating quite a spectacle on quiet ponds and marshes.

idTips.label: Green wing patch
idTips.description: A brilliant emerald-green rectangle on the wing that catches sunlight like a jewel - most visible when the bird stretches or flies, creating an unmistakable flash of color

idTips.label: Male head pattern
idTips.description: Rich rusty-brown head with a curved green stripe extending back from the eye like racing stripes - looks almost painted on in good light

idTips.label: Compact size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than a Mallard, with a proportionally larger head and shorter neck that gives it an almost cute, compact appearance on the water

idTips.label: Fast, erratic flight
idTips.description: Flies in tight flocks with quick, twisting movements that look almost like a school of fish in the air - much more agile than larger ducks

idTips.label: High-pitched calls
idTips.description: Males make a distinctive musical whistle that sounds like 'krick-krick', while females give softer quacking notes - much higher and clearer than a Mallard's voice

idTips.label: Dabbling behavior
idTips.description: Tips forward to feed with tail feathers pointing skyward, often in shallow water where you can hear them quietly splashing and filtering through mud

habitat: Look for Green-winged Teal in shallow freshwater wetlands like ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams with muddy bottoms rich in seeds and small invertebrates. They prefer areas with emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges that provide both food and cover. During migration, they'll also use flooded fields, temporary pools, and even coastal salt marshes throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration brings large flocks in March and April, with males showing off their full breeding plumage including that striking head pattern. Listen for their musical whistling calls as pairs form.
seasonality.summer: Most birds head north to breed, but a few may linger in northern New England wetlands. Any birds seen are likely in quieter molt plumage.
seasonality.fall: September through November brings the heaviest concentrations as birds migrate south, often in mixed flocks with other dabbling ducks. Males begin showing breeding colors again.
seasonality.winter: Small numbers may overwinter in ice-free areas, especially near the coast. Birds appear in basic plumage with more subdued coloring but still show that diagnostic green wing patch.

funFact: Green-winged Teal are speed demons of the duck world - they can reach flying speeds of up to 50 mph and are so agile they can take off almost vertically from the water like tiny helicopters, making them nearly impossible for predators to catch in flight!
confusionNotes: Female Green-winged Teal look very similar to female Blue-winged Teal, but Green-wings are smaller with a shorter, darker bill and lack the white crescent near the eye. Remember: 'Green is keen and compact, blue is bigger with that white eye-brow!'
contextualKnowledge: The North American Green-winged Teal was once considered the same species as the Eurasian Teal, and some scientists still debate whether they should be split or lumped together. You might see them listed as 'American Green-winged Teal' in some older field guides, reflecting this taxonomic uncertainty.
compareHints: Compared to its Mallard relatives, the Green-winged Teal is much smaller and more compact, with proportionally larger wings that allow for faster, more agile flight. Unlike the larger American Black Duck which prefers similar habitats, Green-wings are highly social and form large flocks, while Black Ducks are typically seen in pairs or small groups. The Northern Pintail shares the Green-wing's elegant proportions but is much larger with a distinctive long, pointed tail.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relatives, mallards are noticeably chunkier than the sleek Northern Pintail and much larger than the petite Green-winged Teal.
Compared to mallards, black ducks are consistently darker with no light patches on the body, and males lack the mallard's distinctive green head and white neck ring.
Compared to mallards, pintails are more streamlined with longer necks and blue-grey bills instead of yellow-orange.
Unlike its New England relatives like mallards and black ducks which have more contrasting plumage patterns, the yellow-billed teal has a more uniformly mottled appearance.
